summary: For ages 11–12, teach average speed as a proportional rate linking distance and time, built up from distance = speed × time ('m/s means metres travelled each second') before introducing speed = distance ÷ time. The central threshold is that average speed = TOTAL distance ÷ TOTAL time, including any stationary periods — not the mean of the separate speeds (the mean is only correct when equal time is spent at each speed). Use double number lines and ratio tables to expose the proportional structure and support prediction, connect the calculation to the gradient of a distance-time graph (a single leg's speed is its segment gradient; the whole-journey average is the start-to-end chord gradient), and confront the 'mean of the speeds' and 'ignore the stop' errors directly. A journey-building activity with live, synchronised feedback is the richest approach; a quiz consolidates the procedure; a worked-example reference card scaffolds a single case.
misconceptions: Calculating average speed as the mean of the individual speeds rather than total distance ÷ total time (Third Space Learning).
Forgetting to include stationary periods in the total time when finding average speed.
Reading a value off the vertical axis and calling it the speed instead of finding the gradient.
Treating the formula triangle as the whole concept — procedural recall that blocks proportional reasoning (Susac et al., Phys. Rev. PER).
Language slips: 'constant speed' read as 'always moving', 'steady speed' as 'not too fast'; conflating distance with displacement (Oak National Academy).

activities.title: Build a journey and watch the average speed update
steps: Assemble a trip from segments, choosing a speed for each leg; for the core demonstration use two legs of EQUAL DURATION (e.g. a leg at 8 m/s then an equal-time leg at 4 m/s), and insert optional STOP blocks of a chosen duration.
Before inserting a 20-second stop between the two equal-duration legs, predict the average speed over the whole trip and write down your reasoning.
Insert the stop and observe how the average-speed readout changes; note whether it rose, fell, or stayed the same, and explain why.
Use a double-number-line widget beside the journey to predict: 'keeping this leg's speed, how far would you travel in 10 seconds?' by scaling distance and time together.
Attempt a challenge: adjust the journey to hit a target average speed when one stop is forced into the trip.

State the speed of a single leg with its units and check it against the gradient of that leg's straight segment on the distance-time graph; then note that the whole-journey average speed matches the gradient of the straight line joining the journey's start and end points (the chord), not any single intermediate segment.
activities.insight: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time, and stopped seconds still count in the denominator. With two equal-time legs the mean of the two speeds (here 6 m/s) is genuinely correct; but inserting a stop adds time without adding distance, so the average drops below it — showing that total time, including stops, is what matters. Speed is a proportional rate you can scale to predict new distances and times.

activities.title: Consolidate the calculation and graph reading
steps: Fill in the missing quantity for distance = speed × time and for speed = distance ÷ time rearrangements, attaching correct units each time.
Read the speed of a straight distance-time graph segment by computing its gradient (distance change ÷ time change).
For a multi-leg journey that includes a stop, choose the correct average speed from options that include the 'mean of the speeds' answer, and justify the choice.
Order several graph sections from slowest to fastest by comparing their gradients.
activities.insight: The speed = distance ÷ time procedure can be applied reliably with correct units, average speed over a whole journey is not the mean of the leg speeds, and the gradient of a straight distance-time segment gives that leg's speed.

activities.title: Walk through a worked example as a reference card
steps: Step through one worked journey: reveal the total distance, reveal the total time, then reveal the division and the resulting speed with its units.
Note the unit reminder at each step (metres ÷ seconds = metres per second).
Use the card as a recap aid when stuck on a later calculation.
activities.insight: A single average-speed calculation follows a fixed, checkable sequence: identify total distance, identify total time, divide, and attach units.

activities.title: Measure and reconcile average speed in a real run
steps: Mark two equal 10 m stretches. Have one person jog the first and walk the second while others time each leg.
Before calculating, predict the average speed over the whole 20 m and say WHY.
Calculate average speed from the measured times as total distance ÷ total time, and compare it with your prediction.

Work out each leg's speed from its measured time (10 m ÷ that leg's time), find the midpoint of those two speeds, and discuss why the whole-run average (20 m ÷ total time) is lower than that midpoint whenever the jogging leg was faster than the walking leg.
activities.insight: Over two equal-distance legs, more time is spent on the slower (walking) leg, so the true average speed is pulled below the simple midpoint of the two speeds — the average is weighted by time spent, not by distance.

checkQuestion: A runner covers the first 100 m at 5 m/s, then walks the next 100 m at 2 m/s. A friend says 'the average speed is 3.5 m/s — halfway between 5 and 2'. Is that right? What is the average speed, and how should you work it out?
checkAnswer: No, 3.5 m/s is wrong. Average speed = TOTAL distance ÷ TOTAL time, not the mean of the two speeds. The first 100 m takes 100/5 = 20 s; the second takes 100/2 = 50 s. Total 200 m in 70 s gives an average of about 2.86 m/s. It's below 3.5 because the runner spends MORE time going slowly.
